semantic_note: Schema-level the correspondence holds (a taxon is an organism). Instance-level it fails: the benchmark type is defined to include 'human, mouse or patients', and 90.8% of the BioRED test OrganismTaxon mentions are host-generic terms with ZERO bacterial taxa; the CDM ORGANISM layer is 53.6% microbial by mention and led by 'microbiota'/'gut microbiota'. This is the Species-vs-ORGANISM question and it is the single largest transfer gap in the suite.

Same concept in both corpora. BC5CDR 'Chemical' and BioRED 'ChemicalEntity' both cover drugs, metabolites and named chemical classes; CDM CHEMICAL is the same concept. The only residual difference is granularity (BioRED also tags small molecules that the CDM may file under a different type), not meaning.

BC5CDR 'Disease' is a direct match. BioRED's type is broader (it adds phenotypic features, signs and symptoms) while the CDM has no phenotype type and folds those into DISEASE; the correspondence for the disease core is direct, for the phenotype fringe it is approximate.

GeneOrGeneProduct is a superset that includes genes, mRNAs and protein families. The CDM splits the same region of meaning across PROTEIN and DNA_RNA, so a benchmark hit does not tell you which CDM type it should become. A gene mention scored as a PROTEIN success is a typing error in CDM terms.
SequenceVariant is the nearest BioRED type and it is not the same thing: a variant is a difference in a sequence, not a molecule. No benchmark type corresponds.

CellLine is not CellType. An immortalised line (HeLa, HEK293) is a reagent; a cell type (enterocyte, T cell) is an anatomical class. The benchmark's own label map records the distinction ('cell type != cell line') and maps CellLine to it only because there is no better slot. A high CellLine F1 says nothing about CDM CELL_TYPE extraction.
